Season the thighs hard with salt and pepper. Melt 2 tbsp of the butter in a Dutch oven over medium-high until it foams, then brown the chicken in a single layer on one side only until deeply golden, and move it to a plate.

💡One good side of color is all you need before braising.
Step 2 of 8

Lower the heat to medium, add the onion, the remaining butter, and the caraway seeds, and cook, scraping up the browned bits, until the onion is completely soft and translucent with no crunch left. Put a pot of salted water on to boil while you wait.

Step 3 of 8

Pull the pot entirely off the burner and stir in both paprikas and the marjoram, which should smell sweet and toasty within seconds of hitting the hot fat.

💡Paprika scorches into bitterness in a hot pan, so work off the heat.
Step 4 of 8

Return the pot to medium-low, sprinkle in the flour, and stir until it coats the onions and looks pasty. Whisk in the broth in a steady stream until the sauce is smooth and glossy with no lumps.

Step 5 of 8

Nestle the chicken and its juices back in, cover, and simmer over low until the thighs are fork-tender and the sauce is brick red. Boil the noodles until just tender, drain, and toss them with a pat of butter.

💡Keep it at a lazy bubble, not a rolling boil.
Step 6 of 8

Uncover, pour in the heavy cream, and simmer until the sauce thickens enough that a finger drawn across the back of a spoon leaves a clean line.

Step 7 of 8

Whisk a ladle of the hot sauce into the sour cream in a small bowl until loose, then stir that back into the pot off the heat. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and salt to taste.

💡Tempering is what keeps the sour cream from curdling into grit.
Step 8 of 8

Pile the buttered noodles into shallow bowls, lay the chicken on top, ladle the sauce generously over everything, and grind more black pepper across.

🍛 Tico Casado: Pork Chops with Gallo Pinto
Step 1 of 8

Whisk the Worcestershire, cumin, achiote, brown sugar, half the garlic, and 1/2 tsp black pepper into a thin brown Lizano-style sauce. Rub a third of it over the chops and leave them on the counter while you start the beans.

💡Room-temperature chops sear far more evenly.
Step 2 of 8

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium and cook the onion, bell pepper, and remaining garlic with a pinch of salt until soft, sweet, and browning at the edges.

Step 3 of 8

Add the black beans with all of their canning liquid plus 2 tbsp of the reserved sauce and simmer until the liquid reduces to a dark, syrupy glaze coating the beans. Heat the rice pouch while it bubbles.

💡That bean liquid is what dyes the rice, do not drain it.
Step 4 of 8

Fold the hot rice into the beans until every grain is stained purple-brown, then stir in half the cilantro and pull the pan off the heat. Cover to keep it warm.

💡Stained and glossy, never soupy, is the mark of good gallo pinto.
Step 5 of 8

Slice the plantains on a sharp diagonal about 1/2 inch thick. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a second skillet over medium and fry them until deep caramel and sticky on both cut faces, then drain on a towel and salt immediately.

💡Black skins only, yellow plantains will taste starchy.
Step 6 of 8

Wipe out the first skillet, raise it to medium-high with 1 tsp oil, and sear the chops undisturbed until a dark crust forms and they lift cleanly from the pan.

Step 7 of 8

Flip, brush with the remaining sauce, and cook until the glaze goes tacky and the meat reaches 140F next to the bone.

💡Pull them early, they climb several degrees while resting.
Step 8 of 8

Rest the chops while you plate the gallo pinto, plantains, and a lime wedge on each plate. Slice the chops thick, lay them alongside, and scrape the pan glaze over the top with the rest of the cilantro.

🥙 Me'orav Yerushalmi: Jerusalem Mixed Grill
Step 1 of 8

Slice the thighs into 1/2-inch strips, cut the livers into bite-size pieces, and pat everything very dry. Toss it all with the cumin, turmeric, baharat, coriander, 2 tsp salt, and 1 tsp black pepper until uniformly gold.

💡Dry meat plus a hot pan gives char instead of steam.
Step 2 of 8

Heat 1 tbsp oil in your largest skillet over medium-high until it just begins to smoke, spread half the chicken in a single layer, and leave it alone until the underside is browned and the spices smell toasted. Toss for a minute, then transfer to a bowl.

💡Crowding the pan is the one mistake that ruins this.
Step 3 of 8

Sear the second batch of chicken the same way while you slice the onions, then add it to the bowl.

Step 4 of 8

Add another tablespoon of oil and all the onions with a pinch of salt to the empty skillet over medium-high, scraping up the spiced fond as they release moisture. Cook until they collapse and take on frizzled brown edges.

💡Those stuck-on spices are the whole point of the pan.
Step 5 of 8

Push the onions to the side, drop in the butter, and sear the livers hard until browned outside and barely pink at the center.

💡Overcooked livers turn chalky, so pull them early.
Step 6 of 8

Return all the chicken and its collected juices, add the juice of one lemon and 1/4 cup water, and toss over high heat until the liquid cooks away and everything is glossy and coated.

Step 7 of 8

Whisk the tahini with the juice of the second lemon, a pinch of salt, and cold water added a splash at a time. It will seize into a stiff pale paste first, then loosen into a pourable ivory sauce.

💡It always seizes, keep adding water and keep whisking.
Step 8 of 8

Warm the pitas directly over a burner or in a dry pan until they puff and blister, then stuff them with the grill, drizzle heavily with tahini and zhoug, and tuck pickles down the side.

🍳 Macanese Minchi with Crispy Potatoes and Fried Eggs
Step 1 of 8

Film a large nonstick skillet with olive oil and set it over medium-high until the surface shimmers and thins out. Scatter the frozen potatoes in a single loose layer and walk away so the undersides can blister and turn deep gold.

💡Crowding steams them
Step 2 of 8

Toss the potatoes and keep cooking until most faces are crackly and browned, then scrape them onto a plate and salt them while they are hot. Dice the onion and mince the garlic while they finish.

Step 3 of 8

Return the empty skillet to medium-high, add the beef, and press it into one flat slab. Leave it completely undisturbed until the underside forms a dark brown crust that releases from the pan.

Step 4 of 8

Break the beef into rough pebbles with a wooden spoon, then add the onion, garlic, and bay leaves. Stir often until the onion turns translucent at the edges and the garlic smells toasty rather than sharp.

Step 5 of 8

Pour in the soy sauce and Worcestershire, then sprinkle over the brown sugar and umami seasoning. Simmer over medium until the liquid tightens into a dark glaze that clings to the meat instead of pooling.

💡Glaze, don't drown
Step 6 of 8

While the beef glazes, microwave the frozen jasmine rice according to the bag and fluff it with a fork. Fold the crisped potatoes back into the beef right at the end so they stay crunchy.

Step 7 of 8

In a small nonstick pan over medium heat, fry the eggs in a slick of olive oil until the whites are opaque all the way through and the edges go frilly and brown but the yolks still tremble.

Step 8 of 8

Fish out the bay leaves, spoon the minchi over the rice, and slide an egg onto each plate. Finish with the sliced scallions and a last few drops of Worcestershire.

🌿 Sindhi Seyal Murgh, Smothered in Garlic and Cilantro
Step 1 of 8

Pat the chicken very dry, salt it well, and rub it with the turmeric and red chili powder until every piece is stained yellow. Let it sit while you chop the cilantro, garlic, and tomatoes.

💡Dry chicken, better sear
Step 2 of 8

Heat three tablespoons of olive oil in a heavy skillet over medium-high, then add the cumin seeds. Wait until they sizzle steadily, darken a shade, and smell nutty before moving on.

💡Smell them, don't scorch them
Step 3 of 8

Lay the chicken in one uncrowded layer and leave it alone until the undersides are burnished gold and lift cleanly. Flip once and sear the second side.

Step 4 of 8

Add the minced and smashed garlic, the ginger, and the split green chilies. Stir constantly so the garlic goes pale gold and loses its raw bite without burning.

Step 5 of 8

Tip in the tomatoes and crush them against the pan. Cook over medium until they collapse into a thick paste and you see oil beading at the edges of the masala.

💡Oil separating means the masala is ready
Step 6 of 8

Drop the heat to medium-low and stir in the yogurt one spoonful at a time so it never breaks. Cover and simmer until the chicken is fork tender and the sauce has darkened.

Step 7 of 8

Pile in the whole chopped bunch of cilantro and the garam masala, then fold until the greens wilt down and the sauce is thick enough to cling rather than run. Char the naan in a dry skillet while it finishes.

Step 8 of 8

Let the pan rest off the heat so the masala tightens, then serve straight from the skillet with the hot naan for scooping.

🦐 Venetian Shrimp in Saor over Soft Parmesan Polenta
Step 1 of 8

Warm a generous slick of olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low, then add the sliced onions, bay leaves, and a big pinch of salt. Cook, stirring now and then, until the onions collapse into soft ribbons that are sweet and barely blond.

💡Low and slow keeps them sweet, not brown
Step 2 of 8

While the onions soften, bring a pot of salted water to a rolling boil for the polenta and pat the shrimp completely dry on paper towels.

Step 3 of 8

Pour the vinegar into the onions and add the raisins and sugar. Simmer until the sharp vinegar smell mellows into something rounded and the pan looks glossy and nearly syrupy, then stir in the pine nuts.

Step 4 of 8

Rain the polenta into the boiling water while whisking hard so no lumps form, then drop the heat to low. Whisk often until it thickens enough to pull away from the side of the pot.

Step 5 of 8

Beat the parmesan and butter into the polenta until it is loose and creamy, taste for salt, and cover it off the heat so it stays soft.

Step 6 of 8

Toss the dry shrimp with the flour, salt, and pepper. Sear them in one layer in a hot oiled skillet over medium-high until they turn coral pink, curl into loose C shapes, and are opaque at the thickest part.

💡Argentinian reds cook fast, watch closely
Step 7 of 8

Kill the heat, spoon the warm saor over the shrimp, and toss so every piece is coated. Let the pan sit so the vinegar and sweetness soak in.

💡The rest is what makes it saor
Step 8 of 8

Spread the polenta across two warm shallow bowls, pile on the shrimp and onions with all their syrup, and scatter the parsley over the top.

🥥 Honduran Tapado: Garifuna Coconut Chicken and Shrimp Stew
Step 1 of 8

Season the chicken all over with salt and half the cumin. Heat olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the thighs in two batches, undisturbed, until each side wears a deep golden crust.

💡Two batches, or it steams
Step 2 of 8

While the chicken browns, peel and cut the plantains into thick coins and halve the potatoes so everything is ready to go into the pot at once.

Step 3 of 8

Move the browned chicken to a plate, drop the heat to medium, and add the onion, garlic, and fire roasted peppers and onions. Cook, scraping up the brown film on the bottom, until the onion is soft and translucent.

💡Those scraped-up bits are the flavor
Step 4 of 8

Stir in the rest of the cumin, then return the chicken with its juices and add the broth, coconut milk, potatoes, and plantains. Bring it up to a lazy simmer with slow bubbles rather than a hard boil.

💡A hard boil splits coconut milk
Step 5 of 8

Simmer partly covered until a knife slides into the potatoes with no resistance, the plantains turn tender and starchy, and the broth thickens to pale gold. Chop the cilantro and juice the limes while you wait.

Step 6 of 8

Taste for salt, then slip the shrimp under the surface of the stew and cook just until they curl and turn opaque coral through the middle.

💡Pull them early, the pot keeps cooking
Step 7 of 8

Kill the heat and stir in the lime juice and half the cilantro. Let the pot rest so the coconut settles into the broth and the flavors knit together.

Step 8 of 8

Ladle into deep bowls, making sure every serving gets chicken, shrimp, plantain, and potato. Finish with the remaining cilantro and a wedge of lime.

🔥 Balinese Sate Lilit Chicken with Sambal Matah
Step 1 of 8

Mix the ground chicken with the shredded coconut, two tablespoons of the lemongrass paste, the garlic, turmeric, coconut milk, and a heavy pinch of salt. Work it with your hands until it turns tacky and holds its shape when you squeeze a lump, then chill it.

💡Tacky mix means the patties won't crumble
Step 2 of 8

Build the sambal matah while the mixture chills: toss the shallots, chilies, remaining lemongrass paste, the zest and juice of two limes, and salt with your fingertips, bruising the shallots as you go.

💡Bruise, don't mash
Step 3 of 8

Heat the coconut oil in a small pan over medium-high until it ripples and just begins to shimmer, then pour it straight over the sambal so it sizzles on contact and stir it through.

💡Hot oil wakes the raw shallots up
Step 4 of 8

With wet hands, form the chilled chicken into eight oblong patties, pressing them into flat ovals so they sear evenly rather than steam.

Step 5 of 8

Heat a cast iron skillet over medium-high, film it with oil, and lay the patties in without crowding. Leave them completely alone until the undersides build a dark brown, almost charred crust.

Step 6 of 8

Flip, lower the heat to medium, and cook until the patties feel springy in the middle and the juices run clear with no pink at the center.

Step 7 of 8

Heat the frozen jasmine rice while the patties finish, then fluff it and dust it with the Chili Lime Seasoning.

Step 8 of 8

Pile the rice into bowls, lean the charred patties against it, and heap the sambal matah over everything with its oil. Serve with the last lime cut into wedges.

🍋 Austrian Pork Schnitzel with Warm Vinegar Potato Salad
Step 1 of 8

Start the potatoes first: cover them with heavily salted water, bring to a boil, and cook until a knife slides into the middle with no resistance.

💡Salt the water like soup
Step 2 of 8

While they boil, lay the pork between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound it with a heavy pan until each cutlet is thin, even, and noticeably wider than it started.

💡Even thickness means even frying
Step 3 of 8

Set up three shallow dishes with the flour, beaten eggs, and breadcrumbs. Season the pork, then coat each piece in flour, egg, and crumbs, pressing only lightly so the crust can puff away from the meat.

💡Press hard and the coating glues down
Step 4 of 8

Drain the potatoes, slice them into warm coins, and whisk the mustard, vinegar, warm broth, red onion, salt, and pepper together. Pour it over while the potatoes are still steaming and toss, then leave them to soak.

💡Dress them hot so they drink it up
Step 5 of 8

Melt half the butter with a slick of olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high until the foam subsides. Lay in two cutlets and swirl the pan constantly so hot fat washes over the tops and the crust blisters and puffs golden.

💡Keep the pan moving
Step 6 of 8

Flip and fry the second side until it is the deep color of a good pretzel and the edges are crisp and ruffled.

Step 7 of 8

Drain the schnitzel on a wire rack, never on paper, and salt it the second it comes out of the pan. Wipe the skillet, add the remaining butter and oil, and fry the second pair the same way.

💡A rack keeps the bottom crisp
Step 8 of 8

Fold the chives through the potato salad, taste it for vinegar and salt, and serve the schnitzel straight away with lemon wedges to squeeze over the crust.

🌶️ Tunisian Ojja with Merguez and Eggs
Step 1 of 7

Set a wide skillet over medium-high and brown the merguez coins in a bare film of olive oil until they are crusted on both cut sides and the fat runs out bright red.

💡That red fat is the whole base
Step 2 of 7

Lift the sausage out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat behind. Drop the heat to medium, add the garlic, crushed caraway, and coriander, and stir until they smell toasted but the garlic has not colored.

Step 3 of 7

Stir in the tomato paste and harissa and fry them in the fat, pressing them against the pan, until the paste darkens to brick red and smells roasted instead of raw.

💡Frying the paste kills the tinny taste
Step 4 of 7

Add the fire roasted peppers and onions and the diced tomatoes with their juice. Simmer over medium until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a trail that holds. Slice the bread and chop the parsley while it reduces.

Step 5 of 7

Return the sausage and any resting juices, taste for salt, and make four shallow wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon. Crack an egg into each well and season the yolks.

Step 6 of 7

Cover the pan and cook over medium-low until the whites are fully opaque and set but the yolks still wobble when you nudge the handle.

💡Pull it early, carryover finishes the yolks
Step 7 of 7

Shower the whole skillet with parsley and squeeze lemon over the top. Bring it to the table in the pan with the bread for dragging through the sauce.

🍗 Bahamian Brown Stew Chicken with Thyme and Hot Pepper
Step 1 of 8

Season the chicken hard on all sides with salt, pepper, the thyme, and the allspice, then let it sit out while you slice the onion, pepper, and celery.

💡Season early, season heavily
Step 2 of 8

In a wide Dutch oven over medium-high, stir the brown sugar into a thin film of olive oil and swirl until it melts, foams up, and turns the color of dark coffee with a faintly bitter smell.

💡This burnt sugar is the color of the whole dish
Step 3 of 8

Immediately lay in the chicken skin side down in batches, standing back because it will spit, and brown it hard, turning once, until each piece is lacquered mahogany.

Step 4 of 8

Move the chicken to a tray and add the onion, bell pepper, celery, and bay leaves to the pot. Cook, scraping the dark caramel off the bottom, until the vegetables soften and go glossy.

Step 5 of 8

Stir in the tomato paste and hot sauce and cook until the paste turns brick colored and coats the vegetables.

Step 6 of 8

Return the chicken with every drop of its juice, add the potatoes, and pour in enough water to come halfway up the chicken. Bring it to a simmer, cover, and cook until the meat pulls easily from the bone. Heat the rice pouches near the end.

Step 7 of 8

Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, and let the liquid boil down until the gravy is dark and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

💡Taste for salt only after it reduces
Step 8 of 8

Rest the pot off the heat, fish out the bay leaves, and skim any fat from the surface. Spoon the chicken and gravy over the hot rice.

How to buy this
Ahi Tuna Steaks
Trader Joe's Frozen aisle
Around 2 steaks, roughly 6 oz eachSize
About $8-12Rough price

What the package looks like

Flat freezer box or bag holding individually vacuum-sealed deep-red tuna steaks, each portion sealed in its own tight plastic film.

Make sure it's the right one

The steaks should be a deep natural red through the vacuum film with no gray or brown edges and no ice crystals inside the pack.

Easy to grab by mistake

The frozen mahi mahi and swordfish portions come in similar flat boxes in the same freezer section but are pale rather than red.

Worth knowing

Thaw overnight in the fridge still sealed, then pat completely dry and return it to the fridge until the moment you cook it so it stays firm and sears cleanly.

Beef Chuck Roast
Aldi Meat & seafood aisle
Around 2-3 lbSize
About $5-8 per poundRough price

What the package looks like

Thick rectangular roast in a cling-wrapped tray or vacuum pack, marbled with white fat and streaked with connective tissue.

Make sure it's the right one

Buy the whole roast and cube it yourself rather than the pre-cut stew meat, since chuck is well marbled and the trimmed stew cubes are often lean and dry.

Easy to grab by mistake

The bagged stew meat and the leaner round roast sit in the same case and are commonly grabbed instead.

Worth knowing

Leave the intramuscular fat and silvery seams in place when cubing, as they melt down during a long braise and are what makes the meat tender.

Beef Sirloin Or Flank Steak
Aldi Meat & seafood aisle
Around 1-2 lbSize
About $7-12 per poundRough price

What the package looks like

Vacuum-sealed or cling-wrapped tray of a whole flat steak, with flank showing long visible muscle fibers running end to end and sirloin looking thicker and more compact.

Make sure it's the right one

Either cut works here, so pick the one with the deeper red color and no gray patches or pooled liquid in the tray.

Easy to grab by mistake

Skirt steak and flat-iron look similar in the case, and pre-marinated fajita strips are easy to grab instead of plain steak.

Worth knowing

Whichever you buy, note which way the long muscle fibers run and slice across them at the end, as flank in particular turns stringy if cut the wrong way.

Worth knowing

They squash easily, so put them on top of the cart and freeze any you will not use within a few days.
